items.title: Why the Bomb Is Bad for Democracy
items.description: “In August of 1945, the city of Hiroshima was destroyed in about nine seconds by a single atomic bomb.” So begins the 1981 documentary The Day After Trinity , in a voice-over against a black background. “The man responsible for building the bomb was a gentle and eloquent physicist named J. Robert Oppenheimer.” Directed by a young filmmaker named Jon Else and financed by a public-television station in San Jose, The Day After Trinity quickly became a hit across the United States. One of its innovations was to pair the story of the bomb with that of Oppenheimer, foregrounding the contradiction of this “gentle” pacifist giving the nation its greatest weapon of war. As the historian David K. Hecht has argued , Else’s film helped transform Oppenheimer from a Cold War political figure into a symbol of the profound moral dilemmas inherent in the nuclear age. In the years since the documentary premiered, Americans have continued to view Oppenheimer (and, by extension, his bomb) through Else’s lens. American Prometheus , the Pulitzer Prize–winning biography written by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin, repeatedly cites Else’s interview transcripts and largely replicates his approach. Oppenheimer , Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster 2023 film adaption of the book, does much the same. Now Else, at 82, has revisited the bomb, this time in a nonfiction book he’s been working on for 20 years. Yet Frenchman Flat: The Rise and Fall of Atomic Bombs is not another story of the doomed Oppenheimer; Else relies on his own remarkable interviews from almost half a century ago but doesn’t focus on the scientist, and he declines to “relitigate the decision to drop the bomb” on Japan. Neither is Frenchman Flat quite what its publisher is promoting, the “story of a single nuclear bomb” (a 37-kiloton nuke called Priscilla that exploded over Frenchman Flat , a dry lake bed in Nevada, in 1957). That story, though compellingly told, disappears for whole swaths of the text. Instead, much to its credit, the book unspools an unhurried, capacious story of human society’s collective journey to the brink of annihilation, and of the individuals and movements that have, so far, held us back from the edge. It is a major work, highlighting the heroism and the absurdity of our atomic present and this Strangelovian, Lovecraftian thing we call “nuclear policy.” [ Read: The nuclear club might soon double ] Today, the famous Doomsday Clock , which measures the risk of nuclear cataclysm, is at just 85 seconds from midnight, the closest it’s been to Armageddon since the clock’s creation in 1947. After decades of disarmament, Russia, China, France, and several other nuclear powers are rapidly expanding their arsenals, while Germany, South Korea, Japan, and others are considering developing their own programs. The agreements that long ago halted U.S. and Russian testing recently expired. Donald Trump has been expressing an alarming interest in the use of nuclear weapons for decades . Among Else’s most important accomplishments is recognizing how crucial secrecy has been to the maintenance of nuclear stockpiles. Since the bomb was first developed, the U.S. government has denied the public basic facts about atomic weapons. “The extreme secrecy surrounding almost everything concerning nuclear weapons impeded effective democratic debate for decades,” one report quoted by Else concluded . The bomb, in other words, is bad for democracy, just as democracy is bad for the bomb. The tight grip on information goes back to the beginning—to the Manhattan Project , which brought hundreds of scientists and their families to the New Mexico desert to build an unprecedented weapon. At the height of World War II, the U.S. military concluded that the decision to develop a bomb could not be subject to public debate. Even among members of the U.S. Congress, the historian Alex Hellerstein has calculated , only about 1 percent were brought into the loop. In 1943, the wartime Office of Censorship banned media references to “war experiments,” and officials issued false or misleading responses to press inquiries. Thus, when a bomb exploded onto Hiroshima and “instantly broiled the skin of every person in the open within half a mile,” in Else’s appropriately gruesome phrasing, almost everyone on the planet was genuinely shocked. But that was wartime—and the cessation of hostilities generated new complexities. Could this degree of unaccountability really persist in a time of peace? Else’s interview subjects felt that it shouldn’t. Within weeks of Japan’s surrender, hundreds of Manhattan Project scientists put out a statement calling for “free and enlightened public discussion” of atomic power. Oppenheimer and liberal members of Harry S. Truman’s administration quickly proposed a plan to place control of all nuclear materials and weapons in the hands of the United Nations. As the historian Daniel Immerwahr has noted , much of the scientific community went so far as to seek a “global government” to regulate the bomb. Today this idea might seem unthinkable, but in the ’40s, the notion enjoyed the support of such wild-eyed radicals as Winston Churchill, Richard Nixon, John F. Kennedy, and Ronald Reagan. The postwar constitutions of France and Italy explicitly countenanced a future global body that would trump their own sovereignty. Else cites polls suggesting that about two-thirds of Americans supported some version of this concept. [ Read: What Trump doesn’t understand about nuclear war ] It did not come to pass. U.S. leaders waffled on the idea, and eventually the U.S.S.R., hastily developing a bomb of its own, rejected it. What, then, to do with America’s swelling nuclear arsenal? Many elected officials feared that some “dashing lieutenant colonel” might go rogue with a nuke or three, and so in 1946, Congress passed the Atomic Energy Act, taking control of the bomb away from the military and placing it solely in the hands of the president. Given the trigger-happy proposals floated by many within the military brass in the years to follow, this structure may well have saved countless lives, but it hardly provided for democratic accountability, much less actual arms control. The historian Garry Wills has powerfully argued that the postwar nuclear chain of command altered the United States “down to its deepest constitutional roots,” giving the president exclusive and unfettered power far beyond the comprehension of our country’s founders. Kennedy, for one, considered the presidential nuclear prerogative “insane.” Much of Frenchman Flat is devoted to documenting the insanity that resulted from a nuclear-powered state (and, soon, states) freed from checks and balances and uninterested in public debate. There was no public hearing concerning the U.S. decision to start exploding nuclear bombs in Nevada in 1951; the state’s governor heard about it only a week before the first bomb fell. For years thereafter, the government insisted that nuclear fallout was safe, even as kids across the desert West started receiving leukemia diagnoses. Decades later, studies estimated that as many as 212,000 cases of cancer resulted from U.S. nuclear testing. Meanwhile, behind closed doors, the global superpowers were accelerating the arms race. Both the Americans and the Soviets seriously considered nuclear testing on the moon. The first U.S. test of a hydrogen bomb (hundreds to thousands of times stronger than an atom bomb) was in 1952, and the first Soviet H-bomb test followed in 1953. When a government committee chaired by Oppenheimer recommended strongly against the development of the H-bomb, the Atomic Energy Commission buried the report by classifying it as secret. The H-bomb’s existence became public only after a congressman inadvertently disclosed it on live television. Even Truman hadn’t learned of the “super bomb” until years after its development began. Over the course of the 1950s, as information leaked, public opposition to nuclear testing spread. Impelled by increasing discontent, the Americans and Soviets tentatively entered arms-control discussions. In 1963, they agreed to halt aboveground nuclear testing (underground testing would cease 30 years later). Dozens of countries suspended in-progress nuclear programs. “We are alive to discuss these things thanks in large measure to the grand patchwork of treaties, agreements, and unilateral actions,” Else writes. [ Read: The president’s weapon ] Yet the nuclear peace has always been a fragile one. At least twice, full-scale nuclear war has likely been averted only because a single individual—Vasily Arkhipov in 1962 and Stanislav Petrov in 1983—decided to stand in the way. The U.S. and Russia still have about 5,000 bombs apiece, more than enough to end human civilization. Only voluntary forbearance precludes renewed testing or development or, for that matter, the deployment of intercontinental ballistic missiles and B-2 stealth bombers that are always at the ready. The oceans still teem with nuclear submarines, Else notes, “each boat packing more firepower than what was spent in all the wars in history.” The “nuclear club,” according to an essay in this magazine, is on track to double. Remarkably, Else concludes Frenchman Flat on a note of ambivalence about this unstable status quo. “I have come to appreciate deterrence and understand that until we learn differently our bombs may save us from their bombs,” Else writes. Global abolition, the goal of generations of peace activists, including Martin Luther King Jr. and Pope Leo XIV, is, he adds, “unrealistic.” He shares this perspective with several of his interview subjects, who are international negotiators—members in good standing of what Else labels the “diplomatic bomb squad.” At the same time, he recognizes the absurdity of the nuclear buildup. “Why are you so concerned with saving lives?” he quotes one U.S. general as having said in 1963. “Look, at the end of the war, if there are two Americans and one Russian, we win.” Ultimately, Else does not recommend a path out of the nuclear quagmire (which in fairness was not the task he set for himself). In any event, our international institutions are presently far too weak to provide the supranational control envisioned by mid-century luminaries, and a good number of our current world leaders are almost uniquely ill-suited to steer political bodies that are armed to the teeth. Yet Frenchman Flat does provide some directional cues toward a safer future. Integral to an awareness of nuclear dangers is an end to the regime of secrecy—or at least substantial reform. Democratic oversight of this greatest weapon of war is impossible if the people are deprived of basic information. Of course, democracy is not a sufficient condition for disarmament, much less abolition. The H-bomb was popular with the American public at moments of peak anti-Soviet fervor, just as 70 percent of South Koreans, facing a nuclear regime to the north, want the bomb today. Nonetheless, popular discontent, often driven by leaked information, has historically curbed the nuclear ambitions of many of the most martial leaders. It is reasonable to imagine that even more awareness would spur even more opposition. Sunlight alone will not solve the problem of nuclear proliferation. The aim of the abolitionists, realistic or not, has always been not just to eliminate the bombs but also to alter the conditions that might lead countries to use them. The prospect of a future free of mushroom clouds, they believe, is inseparable from a global order built on cooperation and democracy.

items.title: Pêche côtière : les débarquements au port de Mehdia reculent de 35% à fin août
items.description: Les débarquements de la pêche côtière et artisanale au niveau du port de Mehdia ont atteint 7.906 tonnes (T) à fin août, en baisse de 35% par rapport à la même période de l'année précédente, selon l'Office national des pêches (ONP). La valeur marchande de ces captures a chuté de 49 % pour s’établir à 43,4 millions de dirhams (MDH) à fin août dernier, contre 85,06 MDH à fin août 2025, précise l'Office dans son récent rapport sur les statistiques de la pêche côtière et artisanale au Maroc. Par espèce, les quantités de poissons pélagiques débarquées ont baissé de 34 % au cours des huit premiers mois de cette année, soit 7.754 T pour une valeur estimée à 33,87 MDH, contre 11.810 T/ 43,62 MDH à fin août 2025. Les débarquements de poissons blancs, en revanche, ont progressé de 16% en volume, atteignant 18 T contre 16 T une année auparavant, tandis que leur valeur s’est située à 665.000 DH, contre 773.000 DH, soit une baisse de 14%. Concernant les céphalopodes, les quantités débarquées ont accusé une importante baisse de 74 % à 101T pour des recettes de 7,76 MDH (-80 %), tandis que les débarquements des crustacés ont marqué une hausse de 53 % à 31T, générant des revenus de 1,09 MDH (+29 %). Au niveau national, les débarquements des produits commercialisés de la pêche côtière et artisanale se sont établis à 723.490 T à fin août dernier, en hausse de 6% par rapport à la même période de l'année précédente. En valeur, ces débarquements ont augmenté de 1% à près de 7,44 milliards de dirhams (MMDH) contre environ 7,37 MMDH en glissement annuel. The post Pêche côtière : les débarquements au port de Mehdia reculent de 35% à fin août appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: IJM urges Ghana government to increase and protect child protection funding
items.description: The Country Director of International Justice Mission (IJM), Anita Budu, has called on the government to prioritise financing for child protection as a strategic investment in Ghana’s development. She said adequate and protected funding was necessary to enable institutions responsible for protecting vulnerable children to effectively carry out their mandates. Speaking on the theme “Beyond Policy: Financing Child Protection to Secure Every Child’s Future” at the Mensvic Hotel, on September 17, Anita Budu cited UNICEF research which showed that Ghana’s core child protection spending in 2024 was equivalent to approximately GH¢7 per child per year. She said the figure was based on the budget of the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, excluding the social protection component. According to her, the low level of investment in child protection was particularly concerning when compared with the economic cost of child abuse in Ghana. She noted that previous UNICEF reports had estimated the annual economic cost of child abuse in Ghana at between US$223 million and US$347 million. She called on the government to consider a number of short- to long-term measures to strengthen child protection financing. “We urge governments to prioritise child protection financing as a strategic investment in Ghana’s development,” she said. She said this should include increased and protected allocations for institutions with critical child protection responsibilities. These, she listed, include the Department of Social Welfare, the Labour Department, the National Commission for Civic Education (NCCE), the Human Trafficking Secretariat, and the Human Trafficking Fund. Ms Budu stressed that institutions mandated to protect children could only effectively perform their duties if they were adequately resourced. “If we truly intend to protect vulnerable children, the institutions entrusted with these responsibilities must have the resources to do so effectively,” she said. She therefore urged the government to ensure that funding for child protection was not only increased but also protected to enable the relevant institutions to sustain interventions aimed at safeguarding vulnerable children. The IJM Country Director said sustained investment in child protection was essential to securing the future of children and addressing the wider social and economic consequences associated with child abuse.

items.title: Ondo confirms 48 deaths, 182 cases from suspected alcohol poisoning
items.description: Ondo State Government has confirmed the deaths of 48 persons from the consumption of a local alcoholic drink suspected to be contaminated with methanol. The Commissioner for Health, Dr Banji Ajaka, said this in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) on Thursday in Akure. Ajaka said 182 cases have been reported at medical facilities across Odigbo and Irele Local Government Areas of the state. He said Irele Local Government Area of the state had emerged as the latest flashpoint of the incident, with two communities of Idogun and Gbogunron affected. Ajaka said the source of the deaths had been linked to the consumption of substances suspected to contain methanol. “The source of the death is linked to consumption of suspected methanol. The urine sample from the victims is pointing at suspected methanol,” he said. The commissioner said health authorities and other relevant agencies were still investigating the source of the suspected methanol consumption in the two communities. “We are still looking for the source of consumption in the two communities in Irele Local Government Area,” he said. Ajaka said the state government had strengthened its response to the incident through collaboration with relevant federal and state agencies. “The state government is working with the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, World Health Organisation, National Drug Law Enforcement Agency, Department of State Service, Police, and Amotekun Corps, and the local government to prevent further escalation of the incident,” he said. He said the multi-agency response was aimed at identifying the source of the suspected toxic substance, containing the incident and preventing further deaths. Methanol is a toxic form of alcohol that can cause severe poisoning and death when consumed. The development has raised concern in the state as health authorities continue surveillance and investigations in affected communities. NAN reports that Ajaka had earlier confirmed 29 deaths in communities within Odigbo Local Government Area during a news conference. (NAN) The post Ondo confirms 48 deaths, 182 cases from suspected alcohol poisoning appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Atwima Kwanwoma Assembly reclaims over 30 acres of land degraded by illegal mining
items.description: The Municipal Chief Executive of Atwima Kwanwoma, Grace Agyemang Asamoah, says the assembly has compelled illegal miners in the district to reclaim more than 30 acres of land degraded by their activities. According to her, acres of land had been left with abandoned mining pits before she assumed office, posing serious risks to residents and causing significant environmental damage. She said the Assembly subsequently established a committee to oversee the reclamation exercise, resulting in the restoration of more than 30 acres so far. The DCE expressed optimism that additional degraded lands would be reclaimed by the end of 2027. She disclosed this during a tour of some reclamation sites in the area to assess progress made so far. “Today, I am very happy about the extent of the reclamation exercise so far. Previously, all the roads leading to Nweneso I, II and III were degraded and environmentally unsafe. Now, the affected areas have been covered, and we will begin palm plantation activities,” she said. Madam Grace Agyemang Asamoah further cautioned illegal miners against returning to the reclaimed sites, warning that offenders would be arrested. She said the Assembly had put measures in place to protect the reclaimed lands from renewed illegal mining and preserve them for future generations and other productive uses. The District Environmental Health Officer, Ernest Boakye, also said the reclamation exercise was gradually helping to restore the district’s ecosystem. “The degraded lands are gradually regaining their nutrients and, in the coming years, could be suitable for farming activities,” he said. He therefore called on residents, assembly members and the traditional authorities in the Atwima Kwanwoma Municipality to collaborate with the government and the Assembly to ensure that all degraded lands are fully restored.

items.title: University of Ghana warns 2026/27 applicants against admission scammers
items.description: The University of Ghana has cautioned prospective students against admission scammers following the release of its undergraduate admissions for the 2026/2027 academic year. In a statement issued on Thursday, September 17, the University stressed that its admission process cannot be influenced by any individual or intermediary, urging prospective students to be wary of anyone who claims they can secure admission on their behalf. Applicants have specifically been advised not to make payments, offer gifts or provide favours to individuals who promise to influence or guarantee their admission. The University said applicants should rely on official channels to verify their admission status and obtain accurate information about the admissions process. Applicants can check their admission status through the University’s official admissions portal. To provide further assistance, an Admissions Assistance Desk has opened at the Sports and Wellness Directorate and will operate from Thursday, September 17, to Friday, October 2. The desk will be available from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Monday to Friday, and from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. on Saturdays. The University encouraged applicants with admission-related enquiries to use the designated assistance desk and official admissions portal rather than relying on third parties.

items.title: Face aux Houthis, l’Arabie saoudite se retrouve à court d’alliés
items.description: L'Arabie saoudite se retrouve confrontee a une equation militaire delicate au Yemen, alors que les Houthis multiplient les attaques contre le royaume et ont realise ces derniers jours d'importantes avancees sur le littoral de la mer Rouge. Le 17 septembre, Riyad cherche a contenir cette offensive sans replonger dans une intervention terrestre comparable a celle lancee en 2015. La situation s'est brutalement deterioree avec la progression des Houthis vers Bab el-Mandeb, passage strategique reliant la mer Rouge au golfe d'Aden. Le mouvement soutenu par l'Iran s'est empare de plusieurs positions et îles, tandis que les forces yemenites soutenues par Riyad ont recule. Selon Reuters, les Houthis avaient discretement mobilise environ 100 000 combattants, une preparation qui aurait echappe aux renseignements saoudiens et a leurs allies. Riyad sans option militaire Pour Riyad, le probleme est egalement energetique. Des attaques de drones attribuees a des milices pro-iraniennes en Irak ont provoque l'arret de l'oleoduc Est-Ouest, qui permet d'acheminer le petrole des champs de l'est du royaume jusqu'au port de Yanbu en contournant le detroit d'Ormuz. Dans le meme temps, les missiles et drones houthis frappent de nouveau le territoire saoudien. Or, les soutiens exterieurs restent limites. Les etats-Unis ne souhaitent pas participer directement a une nouvelle offensive au Yemen, tandis que plusieurs puissances occidentales excluent egalement un engagement militaire direct. Riyad a sollicite plusieurs partenaires pour renforcer sa defense aerienne, notamment l'egypte, la France, le Royaume-Uni et le Pakistan. Une intervention massive comporterait cependant le risque d'intensifier encore les frappes houthies contre les infrastructures energetiques saoudiennes. a l'inverse, accepter durablement leurs gains renforcerait leur position au Yemen et autour de Bab el-Mandeb, par lequel transite une partie importante du commerce maritime mondial. Onze ans apres le debut de son intervention au Yemen, Riyad retrouve ainsi un dilemme familier : relancer une guerre coûteuse dont elle avait cherche a sortir depuis la treve de 2022, ou privilegier une negociation avec un mouvement houthi aujourd'hui militairement plus puissant.

items.title: GRIDCo gives Ejisu occupants under high-tension lines 30 days to vacate
items.description: The Ghana Grid Company Limited (GRIDCo) has commenced a sensitisation and eviction exercise in the Ashanti Region to clear all human activities and structures from areas under its high-voltage transmission lines. The exercise, which is being carried out in collaboration with relevant state agencies, is aimed at preventing encroachment on the transmission corridor, which poses serious safety risks. This follows a recent incident at Ashaiman in the Greater Accra Region where a fuel tanker exploded, and parts of the tanker flew and dented one of GRIDCo’s transmission towers. Speaking to the media, the Director of Land Management at GRIDCo, Engineer Bismark Anane, said such incidents underscore the urgent need to keep the transmission corridor free from human activities, especially trading in highly flammable materials, to safeguard lives and property. “The Minister for Energy issued the directive following a recent incident at Ashaiman where a fuel tanker exploded and part of it flew and dented one of the transmission towers. So, to prevent a recurrence of such incidents, a one-month period has been given for occupants living within the right-of-way of the transmission lines to vacate voluntarily,” he said. According to him, continuous occupation of the Right of Way not only endangers the lives of encroachers but also compromises the integrity of GRIDCo’s transmission infrastructure and hinders safe access for routine maintenance and emergency repair works. He noted that high-voltage transmission lines carry extremely high currents, and any close human activity within the corridor could result in electrocution, fire outbreaks, and widespread power disruptions. He stressed that the enforcement is not intended to punish anyone but to enforce safety regulations and ensure reliable power transmission across the country. At Ejisu, where the exercise has started, residents, traders, artisans and commercial drivers operating directly under and around the high-tension lines have been given a 30-day ultimatum to vacate the area. During an engagement with affected occupants, GRIDCo clarified that not all affected persons will automatically qualify for compensation. He explained that compensation will only be considered for affected occupants who can produce proper and verifiable documentation establishing their legitimate interest in the land they occupy. He said persons who settled in the area without lawful authority or official documentation cannot be compensated, as their occupation is considered illegal. GRIDCo has therefore urged all occupants within the transmission corridor to take note of the 30-day notice and make the necessary arrangements to relocate before the enforcement of the directive. Meanwhile, affected occupants have expressed mixed reactions to the directive. While some say they are ready to comply with the order, they are appealing to GRIDCo and the authorities to provide alternative places for them to relocate before any eviction or demolition is carried out. Some blamed the Ejisu Municipal Assembly, saying they were allowed to settle and operate in the area for years despite the visible presence of the transmission lines and were even collecting tolls and levies from them. Others claimed they occupied the area long before the transmission lines were installed and therefore want their circumstances to be considered on humanitarian grounds. According to them, a forceful eviction without an alternative place will lead to loss of homes, collapse of businesses and livelihoods, as many of them depend solely on activities within the enclave for survival. They have therefore appealed to the government to intervene to ensure a humane approach to the exercise.

items.title: Sandbondtenga/Éducation: l’école primaire publique de Nionko retrouve son village d’origine après deux ans de délocalisation
items.description: BURKINA-SANDBONDTENGA-ÉDUCATION-RESILIENCE Sandbondtenga/Éducation: l’école primaire publique de Nionko retrouve son village d'origine après deux ans de délocalisation Pissila, 15 sept. 2026 (AIB) – L’école primaire publique de Nionko a retrouvé, mardi 15 septembre 2026 son site d’origine après deux années de déplacement à Pissila pour cause d’insécurité. Ce retour a été marqué par la rentrée administrative, tenue dans une atmosphère de soulagement. Le retour des populations à Nionko, favorisé par les efforts des Forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS) et des Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP), a ouvert la voie à celui de l’école. « l'école nous a manqué deux ans durant. Certains enfants ont dû abandonner les classes. », a expliqué le président du conseil d'école, Sournoma Sawadogo. Pour lui, c'est une joie pour tous de voir l’école du village reprendre vie. La rentrée administrative a réuni l’ensemble des enseignants de l'école et a été marquée par la lecture commentée des instructions officielles, la répartition des classes et des tâches, ainsi que le recrutement des nouveaux élèves. Selon le directeur de l'école, Sibiri Roland Ouédraogo, cette reprise marque une étape importante pour la communauté éducative. « Cette rentrée est très importante pour nous. Nous avons accompli le devoir en rejoignant les populations retournées avec le service scolaire. Nous espérons le soutien des communautés pour assurer une éducation de qualité », a-t-il déclaré. L’école primaire publique de Nionko, de la Circonscription d’Éducation de Base (CEB) de Pissila 1, avait été délocalisée en 2024. A cause de l’insécurité, élèves, enseignants et populations avaient été contraints de quitter le village pour s'installer à Pissila le chef-lieu de la commune. En cette rentrée scolaire 2026-2027, l’école primaire publique de Nionko est de retour dans son village d’origine. Ce retour témoigne de l’amélioration de la situation sécuritaire dans plusieurs localités du Burkina Faso. Agence d'Information du Burkina KAO/aio/bak

items.title: Pakistan women survive Thailand scare to make Asian Games semi-finals
items.description: Pakistan survived a serious scare to win the quarter-final of the Asian Games Women’s Cricket Competition against Thailand by three wickets at the Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin, Japan on Thursday. Put in to bat by Pakistan, Thailand posted 91 runs in the designated 11 overs following rain delay before Pakistan went deep and left only two balls to spare as they crossed the finish line. Fatima Sana’s side had also lost seven wickets in the process and it was the captain’s 21 off 13 after opener Shawal Zulfiqar’s 25 off 14 that kept Pakistan in the game, despite the usually talismanic Fatima losing her wicket before finishing the job. Thailand had got off to a brisk start, scoring 41 runs in the powerplay on the back of a productive 24 off 22 balls from Nannapat Koncharoenkai. Fatima had drawn first blood with the ball, dismissing Natthakan Chantham for six runs. Koncharoenkai took the attack to Tuba Hassan and Umm-e-Hani, hitting the latter for 14 runs off the eighth over, as she stitched a solid 65-run stand with Phannita Maya. A dropped catch by wicket-keeper Gul Feroza and lapses in the field aided Thailand as they raced to 72 off 9 overs, when Maya was retired out on a 16-ball-15. Nauremol Chaiwai smoked Nashra Sandhu for a six and a four before falling to her on the next ball, getting caught by Fatima. It was the skipper only who finally dismissed Koncharoenkai in the last over of the shortened innings, the batter narrowly missing out on a half-century as she was trapped lbw for a 38-ball-49; Fatima ended with figures of two for 22 in her three-over spell. Shawal starts strong Shawal, and fellow opener Gul Feroza, gave Pakistan a strong start to the chase, scoring two boundaries in the first over. She followed it up with a six off Maya’s bowling in the second. Both Gul and Shawaal were dropped in the third and fourth overs respectively, but the openers kept the scoreboard ticking before Shawal was caught and bowled by Onnicha Kamchomphu, who took a well-judged catch. The first wicket triggered a collapse which saw Thailand take four wickets in 13 balls. Ayesha Zafar came out to bat at one-drop, and was dismissed almost immediately, falling in the next over to Suleeporn Laomi, with Thailand pulling back some control as Pakistan finished the fifth over at 39-2. Kamchomphu picked up her second wicket as Gul was stumped by keeper Koncharoenkai, with Pakistan finding themselves in a serious wobble at 43-3, which turned into 47-4 as the experienced Aliya Riaz went boundary-and-out in the same over. Thailand conceded just one run in the seventh over, tightening their grip on the match as Pakistan ominously sunk further. Fatima, batting at number four, then reeled back momentum by hitting Kamchomphu for three fours and a six in the ninth over, joined by a six off the batting of Eyman Fatima. The captain fell on the first ball of the following over, and was followed by Eyman in the next as Pakistan again found themselves in some bother at 76-7. A six and a four off Sunida Chaturongrattana’s bowling by Tuba Hassan took the equation to less than run-a-ball for Pakistan, and following her dismissal to the same bowler, Umm-e-Hani and Eman Naseer took Pakistan over the line in the last over. Earlier, China’s cricket return to the Asian Games for the first time in 12 real came to a halt before a ball was even bowled. Their quarter-final fixture against Bangladesh in Nagoya was first delayed due to a wet outfield, and eventually called off without a toss. Bangladesh proceed to the semi-finals, owing to their higher seeding. Both semi-finals will be held on Sept 20 at Nisshin. Pakistan will take on the winners of tomorrow’s quarter-final clash between Malaysia and Sri Lanka, while Bangladesh will meet the winners of the later fixture between India and Japan.

items.title: Nice : Christian Estrosi visé par une enquête pour détournement de fonds publics
items.description: L'ancien maire de Nice se trouve au cœur d'une procedure judiciaire ouverte fin août pour detournement de fonds publics. 🚨 NOTES DE FRAIS D'ESTROSI : NOTRE COMBAT DE DEUX ANS ABOUTIT ENFIN À UNE ENQUÊTE 🚨 🧶👇 (1/5) https://t.co/88vpnoH0aE pic.twitter.com/NNAM3rdA74 — Transparence Citoyenne (@TransparenceCit) September 17, 2026 Le signalement, transmis fin juillet par eric Ciotti au titre de l'article 40, porte sur l'absence de pieces justificatives pour une partie de ses notes de frais de representation. Un dossier deja signale par une association Peu apres son election en mars 2026 sous la banniere UDR-RN, eric Ciotti avait somme son predecesseur de produire les justificatifs manquants. Face au silence, il a saisi le parquet. L'association Transparence citoyenne avait de son cote depose une plainte, relevant plus de 312 000 euros de frais rembourses sans justificatif au profit de Christian Estrosi entre 2016 et 2025. 👉 UNE AFFAIRE ENTAMÉE EN 2024 (2/5) Depuis 2024, nous avons demandé à Christian Estrosi la communication de ses notes de frais. Sans jamais obtenir de réponse de sa part, nous avons finalement su, via le nouvel exécutif niçois, qu’il avait engagé 312 023,33 € de frais de… — Transparence Citoyenne (@TransparenceCit) September 17, 2026 Le procureur de la Republique, Damien Martinelli, a confirme mercredi l'ouverture de l'enquete, validant une information de Nice-Matin. L'avocat de Christian Estrosi, maître Matthieu Avril, denonce « un contexte d'acharnement et de mises en cause repetees » de la part d'eric Ciotti. Il assure que son client a toujours veille « a la bonne utilisation des deniers publics » et a regulierement reverse a la metropole la part non utilisee de son enveloppe. En realite, l'ancien maire semble avoir ete lâche depuis longtemps par ses allies politiques, a commencer par les LR et Bruno Retailleau qui avaient renonce a le soutenir lors de l'election municipale de 2026 face a eric Ciotti . Interroge precedemment, l'ancien maire avait indique que ces frais correspondaient a des repas avec des investisseurs ou des personnalites pour faire avancer les dossiers de la ville. Christian Estrosi, desormais proche d'edouard Philippe, fait deja l'objet de plusieurs enquetes sans etre mis en examen, notamment sur la reconstruction apres la tempete Alex, la securisation de la Promenade des Anglais le soir de l'attentat de 2016 , et la gestion d'evenements lies aux Grands Prix de Formule 1 .

items.title: Musique guinéenne : L’artiste Azaya plaide pour l’apaisement et l’unité entre fans et artistes
items.description: L’artiste guinéen, Mohamed Kamissoko, connu sous le pseudonyme d’Azaya, a lancé un appel à l’apaisement à l’endroit de ses fans et, plus largement, des amoureux de la musique guinéenne. Il a appelé mercredi à mettre fin aux insultes visant les artistes et leurs familles, au nom de l’unité et de la cohésion dans le milieu culturel. Se présentant comme un griot et un ambassadeur de la culture africaine et mandingue, Azaya a rappelé que le rôle du griot est notamment de contribuer à la paix et à la cohésion sociale. « L a musique guinéenne est l’une des plus riches de l’Afrique. Nous avons besoin de nous unir, de conjuguer un même verbe pour le bien de la culture guinéenne », a-t-il déclaré. S’adressant particulièrement à ses fans, Mohamed Kamissoko les a exhortés à cesser les injures dirigées contre d’autres artistes guinéens. « Je lance un appel à tous mes frères, mes adorables et paisibles Azaya Boss, de faire un effort d’arrêter toutes sortes d’injures à l’encontre de qui que ce soit, à l’encontre de n’importe quel artiste guinéen », a-t-il déclaré. Pour l’artiste, les critiques et les suggestions ont leur place dans le débat autour de la musique, mais les attaques personnelles et les insultes ne contribuent pas à son développement. Il a également présenté ses excuses aux différentes familles qui auraient été touchées par les insultes liées à ces tensions, avec une attention particulière aux femmes. « La femme, c’est la source de vie. Ce sont nos mamans, ce sont nos sœurs, ce sont nos filles. Donc elles méritent le respect, la considération, mais surtout la grandeur », a-t-il insisté. Au nom de son équipe, Azaya a enfin présenté ses excuses aux fans de la musique guinéenne ainsi qu’aux personnes qui auraient été affectées par ces débordements. Il a appelé les acteurs de la musique à privilégier l’unité afin de poursuivre le développement de la culture guinéenne. « Il faut qu’on se donne la main, il faut qu’on bouge ensemble. Vive la musique guinéenne, vive la culture guinéenne », a-t-il conclu.

items.title: 2e jeux de l’AES : Le Burkina Faso termine en tête avec 125 médailles
items.description: 2e jeux de l’AES : Le Burkina Faso termine en tête avec 125 médailles Ouagadougou, 16 sept. 2026 (AIB) – Le Burkina Faso a terminé en tête de la deuxième édition des Jeux de la Confédération des Etats du Sahel (AES), avec 125 médailles, devant le Niger qui en a obtenu 72 et le Mali 54, à l’issue de dix jours de compétition, d’échange entre jeunes et de valorisation du patrimoine sportif sahélien, dans la capitale burkinabè. Au total, 376 athlètes et 164 encadreurs du Burkina Faso, du Mali et du Niger ont pris part aux compétitions dans onze disciplines sportives, notamment le football, le handball, la lutte traditionnelle, la boxe, le judo, l’athlétisme, le tir à l’arc et le kung-fu wushu. La ministre des Sports, de la Jeunesse et de l’Emploi du Burkina Faso, Annick Lydie Djouma Pikbougoum/Zingué Ouattara, a, pour sa part, relevé la place accordée à des disciplines contribuant à la valorisation du patrimoine sportif sahélien, notamment la lutte traditionnelle et le tir à l’arc. « Un peuple qui connaît sa valeur, qui assume son histoire et qui préserve son identité est un peuple qui avance debout », a-t-elle souligné, invitant les jeunes de l’AES à rester profondément enracinés dans leur culture. Elle a également indiqué aux athlètes qu’ils ne sont pas seulement les bénéficiaires de l’histoire en construction, mais qu’ils en sont les acteurs. Cette deuxième édition achevée mardi 16 septembre à Ouagadougou, a permis aux athlètes des trois pays de se mesurer dans différentes disciplines, tout en favorisant les rencontres entre les jeunesses de la Confédération. La directrice générale des Sports et des Loisirs du Burkina Faso, présidente du comité national d’organisation des Jeux, Wendguété Valérie Badolo/Tapsoba, a salué la mobilisation autour de l’événement. « Votre engagement a permis de transformer une décision en réalité et une ambition en événement », a-t-elle déclaré. Elle a également salué la mobilisation des forces de défense et de sécurité, des services de santé, des bénévoles et de la population burkinabè durant les dix jours de compétition. Avec 125 médailles, le Burkina Faso devance donc le Niger (72) et le Mali (54) au classement final provisoire de cette deuxième édition. La troisième édition des Jeux de l’AES est prévue en 2027 à Niamey, au Niger. Agence d’information du Burkina VAT/yos

items.title: Why it’s harder for female artistes to be successful – Fave
items.description: Nigerian singer Chidozie Godsfavour Ugochinyere, popularly known as Fave, has spoken about the challenges female artistes face in the music industry, saying their success is often judged by their appearance rather than their talent. Fave made the remark during a recent episode of the Afropolitan podcast, where she compared the expectations placed on female artistes with those placed on their male counterparts. According to the singer, women in the industry are often expected to meet certain physical and fashion standards before their music receives attention. “It is harder for female artistes to ‘blow.’ Female artistes aren’t measured by talent but by what they wear. If your tummy isn’t flat, people sexualise you,” she said. Fave said the situation has shifted attention away from the music itself, arguing that some female artistes are subjected to scrutiny based on how they look and dress. “It is never really about the music; it is more about people’s sexual desires or their fantasies about you,” she said. Fave described the expectation as problematic, noting that female artistes can be judged on how decently they dress before listeners consider the quality of their music. “And I think that right there is a problem, because it becomes more about how decently you are dressed before people listen to you,” Fave said. The singer also pointed to what she described as a different standard for male artistes, saying they are not subjected to the same level of scrutiny over their appearance. “But when it comes to men, they aren’t held to that same standard,” she added. Despite the challenges, Fave maintained that female artistes continue to make significant contributions to the Nigerian music industry, performing strongly despite the additional expectations placed on them. The post Why it’s harder for female artistes to be successful – Fave appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Guinée: le média impérialiste français France 24 mis en demeure pour avoir qualifié le président Mamadi Doumbouya de « président putschiste »
items.description: GUINEE-MISE-EN-DEMEURE-FRANCE24 Guinée: le média impérialiste français France 24 mis en demeure pour avoir qualifié le président Mamadi Doumbouya de « président putschiste » Ouagadougou, 17 sept. 2026 (AIB)- La Haute Autorité de la Communication (HAC) de Guinée a mis en demeure, mercredi 16 septembre 2026, la chaîne impérialiste française France 24 pour avoir utilisé, dans son édition d’information du mardi 15 septembre 2026, le qualificatif « président putschiste » pour désigner le chef de l’État guinéen, Mamadi Doumbouya. La HAC a jugé cette appellation « inappropriée » et contraire aux exigences d’exactitude, d’impartialité et d’équilibre dans le traitement de l’information. Elle a notamment reproché à la chaîne impérialiste d’ignorer, par cette formulation, la légitimité issue de l’élection présidentielle du 28 décembre 2025 et de la prestation de serment du 17 janvier 2026. La HAC a demandé à France 24 de cesser l’utilisation de termes qu’elle considère comme « inappropriés, dégradants et attentatoires à la dignité des institutions guinéennes » et de procéder aux rectifications nécessaires. Elle a également averti qu’une récidive ou le non-respect de la mise en demeure pourrait entraîner des sanctions prévues par la législation guinéenne. Agence d’Information du Burkina

items.title: NPP rejects current constitutional review process, demands Consultative Assembly
items.description: The opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP) has rejected the current approach to reviewing Ghana’s 1992 Constitution and called for the establishment of a Consultative Assembly to deliberate on the proposed changes. Member of Parliament for Ofoase-Ayirebi, Kojo Oppong Nkrumah, said the scale of the proposed reforms goes beyond what should be treated as routine amendments under Chapter 25 of the Constitution. Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, September 17, 2026, he said the NPP would oppose the proposed amendments in Parliament and campaign against them at the referendum. “The New Patriotic Party therefore rejects this approach being pursued by the NDC government in essentially rewriting the 1992 Constitution,” he stated. Mr Oppong Nkrumah acknowledged that the 1992 Constitution contains provisions that could be improved to strengthen accountability, decentralisation and public institutions. However, he argued that the breadth of the proposals under consideration amounts to a fundamental overhaul of the constitutional order. The Constitution Review Committee’s report contains 206 proposals, comprising 147 proposed amendments to existing provisions and 59 entirely new provisions. Mr Oppong Nkrumah said the proposals affect major areas of governance, including the Executive, Parliament, the Judiciary, independent constitutional bodies and local government. “Amendments to 147 of 299 articles, together with 59 new provisions—that is 206 propositions in all—reaching into the executive, the legislature, the judiciary, independent constitutional bodies, and local government, is not just an adjustment to some provisions of the Constitution. They amount to the overhaul of the Constitution and in substance the enactment of a new one,” he said. He argued that changes of such magnitude should not be processed solely through Parliament and a referendum. “A change of that magnitude cannot be treated as routine business under Chapter 25, to be carried through a parliamentary session and then a referendum.” Mr Oppong Nkrumah also criticised what he described as significant differences between the recommendations of the Constitution Review Committee and the government’s position. He claimed that the government had substituted its own preferences for many of the committee’s recommendations. “Out of the 147 recommendations, about 100 of them—that is 68%—the NDC government has substituted their own preference for the views of the independent committee that the President himself put together,” he alleged. He further accused the government of limiting further consultation on the proposals and said there had been no platform for political parties, organised labour, professional groups and other identifiable groups to resolve areas of disagreement. The government, however, has said the Constitution Review Committee itself undertook extensive consultations, including engagements with more than 21,500 people, 10 thematic stakeholder engagements involving more than 500 experts and practitioners, and consideration of 785 written submissions. The government has also established an 11-member Constitution Review Implementation Committee to examine its position paper alongside the Constitution Review Committee’s report and develop a framework for implementing the proposals. Mr Oppong Nkrumah said the NPP’s preferred approach would involve an expert body developing proposals which would then be subjected to detailed consideration by a broad and representative assembly before they are given legal effect. “A change of this magnitude to the constitutional order of our nation should follow the time-tested path by which Ghana has made every such change. First, the work of an expert body deliberated and settled upon by a broad and representative assembly and only then given the force of law,” he stated. He cited Ghana’s constitutional experiences in 1969, 1979 and 1992 as examples of processes that, in the NPP’s view, provide a basis for broader deliberation. “This is how it was done in 1969, in 1979, and in 1992. And that is what we are calling on the government to respect now,” he said. The NPP’s position adds to calls from other stakeholders for broader consultation on the proposed constitutional changes, including concerns about the process and timeline for implementing the reforms. The government has indicated that amendments to entrenched provisions will ultimately be subjected to a national referendum, while non-entrenched provisions will follow the parliamentary amendment process prescribed by the Constitution.

items.title: Ninth woman found dead in South Africa killing spree
items.description: South African police on Thursday recovered the body of a ninth woman east of Johannesburg in two months, as a string of murders continues to stoke public anxiety. The country has one of the world’s highest homicide rates but the discovery of the women’s bodies, partially naked and battered, has raised fears that a serial killer or group of killers may be operating in the area. Police have imposed a lockdown in Kempton Park in the Ekurhuleni municipality and officers mounted roadblocks after three of the bodies were found this week. A police cordon stretched along the roadside where the latest victim was discovered, drawing clusters of residents who stood watching as investigators combed the scene. Forensic officers in white protective suits moved around the area while the woman’s body lay under a sheet beside the road. “We cannot continue picking up bodies,” deputy police chief Tebello Mosikili told journalists at the scene. The killings have left residents shaken. “This is very scary… because you can say us as woman and children are no longer safe,” said Patience Masa. “I told someone on the phone that, I don’t feel safe, for this to happen in the morning, so we are not safe,” said another resident Zanele Vilakazi. – Copy cat – Police have offered a 400,000 rand ($25,000) reward for any information that could lead to the arrest of the killer or killers, while the Democratic Alliance, the second largest political party in South Africa offered $31,000. Mosikili said offices will investigate whether the Thursday discovery was linked to the earlier murders or if they were dealing with a copycat. Gender-based violence is endemic in South Africa, where one in three women experiences physical or sexual violence during her lifetime, according to the United Nations, despite years of government pledges to tackle it. One of the victims, 38-year-old Elizabeth Moselakgomo, left her eight-year-old daughter at home to go for a jog and never returned. Her body was found on September 12 behind a hotel. Her disappearance drew public attention after fellow runners launched a social media campaign to find her, bringing renewed focus to earlier cases and, later, to the discovery of more bodies. The first victim, a 37-year-old woman, was found naked and bound with cable ties on July 15. A suspect was arrested two days later and appeared in court on Wednesday, police said. Mosikili said the man was a foreigner but could not say from where. The second woman, 32, was found partially clothed on August 24, while a third was discovered naked and in an advanced state of decomposition on September 10. – Declared war – Provincial premier Panyaza Lesufi on Thursday said “someone has declared war against us, and we will push back, we are not going to surrender”.’ President Cyril Ramaphosa on Tuesday said “no stone will be left unturned” to solve the killings, acknowledging “these incidents are causing fear and uncertainty in our communities, and especially among women”. The killings have drawn condemnation from civil society and sporting bodies as calls grow for action on gender-based violence, which South Africa has declared a national emergency. South Africa, a nation of 62 million people, has some of the highest rates of violence against women and children in the world, according to UN Women. AFP The post Ninth woman found dead in South Africa killing spree appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Parliament to open Ghana’s first Parliamentary Museum to the public on September 22
items.description: The Parliament of Ghana is set to open its first Parliamentary Museum to the public on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, in a move aimed at preserving the country’s parliamentary heritage and deepening public understanding of the legislature. According to a press release issued by the Parliamentary Service, the museum will be open to visitors Mondays to Fridays, from 9:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The museum is described as a landmark legacy project of the Speaker of Parliament, Rt. Hon. Alban S. K. Bagbin, and will feature materials documenting the evolution of Ghana’s Parliament and constitutional development. Its collection will include historical photographs, documents and records of parliamentary proceedings, artefacts and memorabilia associated with former Speakers, archival materials on the Legislative Council, and items relating to Ghana’s constitutional milestones. Visitors will also have access to multimedia and interactive exhibits focusing on the law-making process and the history of governance in Ghana. The Parliamentary Service said the museum is expected to serve a broad range of visitors, including students, researchers, tourists, cultural enthusiasts, Members of Parliament and parliamentary staff. For students and researchers, the museum is intended to provide primary-source material for studying Ghana’s parliamentary and constitutional development, while tourists and cultural visitors will have an opportunity to explore aspects of the country’s democratic heritage. Members of Parliament and staff are also expected to benefit from the museum as a repository of institutional memory, while international partners and other legislatures will be able to engage with Ghana’s parliamentary history. Members of the public wishing to visit will be required to book through Parliament’s official website by selecting “Visit” and then “Museum.” Visitors will be notified by message once their requests have been approved. The Parliamentary Service said the establishment of the museum reflects Parliament’s commitment to openness, public education and preserving the nation’s legislative history for future generations.

items.title: Who Made America Poorer and Dirtier?
items.description: At last week’s GOP midterm convention in Dallas, Vice President Vance painted a bleak picture of American life before the second Trump administration: “Two years ago, we have to remember, our nation, ladies and gentlemen, was tired. We were tired of seeing our factories close. We were tired of our neighbors dying of drug overdoses. We were tired of not being able to afford anything. We were tired of seeing the cartels and the criminals given free rein over our great country,” Vance said. “And we were tired of being called racist for noticing that our country was becoming dirtier and poorer and less safe and less prosperous.” Who is responsible for this terrible state of affairs? The opposition party and immigrants, apparently. Vance went on to say, “The Democrat legacy of the last few years was that they bankrupted our country and left us poor. They left our country weaker. They left our border wide open and our communities less safe.” But this account represents a preposterous inversion. Almost every problem Vance lists, the Trump administration has made worse. The administration’s environmental policies have made American water and air dirtier. Its health-care, tariff, and tax policies have worsened inflation and increased the financial burden on most American households, even as incomes have grown. And its public-health policies have led to outbreaks of contagious disease. The Environmental Protection Agency under President Trump has revoked regulations on air pollution—including those on particulate matter that can cause heart and lung disease—after being intensely lobbied by the fossil-fuel industry. It has repealed limits on “forever chemicals” in drinking water, which are linked to cancer and other health problems. The Trump Justice Department scrapped a settlement compelling Alabama to provide adequate sanitation systems to residents living with raw sewage, describing it as “DEI.” After the residents of Jackson, Mississippi, learned they had been drinking lead-tainted tap water, a Trump-appointed federal judge ruled that Americans don’t have a constitutional right to clean drinking water. Although Trump won the 2024 election largely because of Biden-era inflation, he has done everything in his power to make inflation worse. Trump’s arguably illegal and certainly ill-advised war in Iran has led to the closure of strategic shipping waterways, which has provoked a rise in energy prices, which is in turn raising the prices of other goods. Trump’s tariffs worsened inflation by raising the price of imports, and wages seem to be falling behind inflation. To make matters worse, health-care costs are rising rapidly, in part because of the Trump administration’s repeal of Affordable Care Act subsidies in its One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Crime is down. But that’s not because of the Trump administration’s mass-deportation program, whose brutal and indiscriminate tactics have weakened the economy rather than strengthened it. The reality is that immigrants are far less likely than native-born Americans to commit crimes, and crime has been falling steadily since the pandemic-induced spike in 2020 and 2021. Absent significant changes to the space-time continuum, Trump cannot claim credit for a decline in crime that began before Trump even took office, especially with an FBI director who devotes bureau resources to respond to people mocking him on X. Vance called out two women, one of whom was born in Somalia, who defrauded Medicaid of $46 million. But the Trump administration has been happy to pardon fraudsters such as Lawrence Duran, who was sentenced to 50 years in prison for defrauding Medicare of more than $200 million, or Robert Harshbarger Jr., the husband of Republican Representative Diana Harshbarger, who had pleaded guilty to health-care fraud . Last February, Elizabeth Oyer, a former U.S. pardon attorney, told The New York Times that Trump’s pardons had “essentially wiped away about $1 billion in penalties and restitution secured by federal prosecutors in fraud cases.” But the number may be even larger; Democrats on the judiciary committee estimated in August that the number is closer to $2 billion. Safety isn’t just about crime, and in this respect, the Trump administration has tried its best to make the federal government worse at protecting Americans from foreseeable problems. Cuts to public agencies have coincided with outbreaks of infectious and foodborne diseases , to the point that the administration is trying to manipulate numbers to hide measles deaths . I don’t know about you, but I felt safer when I could eat lettuce without thinking about whether it would make me sick. Or berries. Or beef. In fairness, however, not everyone is getting poorer—the top 1 and 0.1 percent of American households have seen their income grow considerably, thanks to the OBBBA’s slashing of taxes on the wealthy; the bottom 50 percent, not so much. This is a trend that began long before Trump—and has been sustained in part by the Democrats’ unwillingness to reverse Republicans’ tax cuts. To the extent that anyone should be happy with the Trump administration’s policies, though, many of its extremely wealthy backers are getting all they paid for and then some. As for everyone else? The country is almost certainly dirtier, poorer, less prosperous, and in some ways less safe than in 2024. But that’s not because of Democrats or immigrants. It’s because of the people currently running the place. They’re really hoping you’ll blame someone else.

items.title: The Empty Promise of Therapy Without a Therapist
items.description: Therapy can involve a lot of words, but it’s often the pauses that matter most. If you transcribed a session, the pauses would look like nothing: beats of silence, extra breaths, slowing down. But these can represent the crux of the practice: entry points into feeling. My job as a psychoanalyst is to listen as much to silence as to words, to be present with the patient while they’re quiet—to stay with them as they allow their feelings to emerge. I was trained across diverse theories and techniques, but in my clinical work I have found that the cornerstone of the process is feeling. The patient’s emotional experience is the destination and the terrain. But I also feel; I am moved. And the work I do with my patients relies on our relationship and our capacity for mutual feeling. In many ways, the history of my field from Freud on has been a growing acknowledgement of the reality of this relationship—moving from the therapist as sealed off and standing apart, toward approaches that view the real human relationship between patient and therapist as the territory where healing happens. Now the rise of the AI therapist is upon us. The growing cadre of AI mental-health services tend to avoid using words like therapist and therapy . They say that they do not replace professional help and that they can refer users to human therapists if needed. But their positioning as a therapy-like service is clear. In June, the therapy giant Talkspace launched its AI mental-health agent, Tee, “developed to help individuals navigate life’s daily mental health challenges.” Then there’s Ash, which offers to support your “emotional wellbeing,” helping you to “connect the dots between thoughts, feelings, and behaviors.” Abby promises to be “warm, thoughtful, and direct” and to help you “work through the kinds of everyday emotional challenges that often go unspoken.” And Headspace’s Ebb advertises: “Stressed at work? Family drama? Trouble sleeping? Ebb can help you unpack what’s on your mind and move forward with more clarity.” When I reached Talkspace for comment, a company spokesperson told me in an email that Tee is “absolutely not a replacement for human therapy. It is a safe AI mental-health guide that can be used to talk through situations like stress, anxiety, relationships, life challenges, and personal growth.” AI therapy is a radical move, and we need to reckon with what happens when we turn to therapists who cannot feel. Therapy and AI have been intertwined since the technology’s beginnings. One of the first chatbots, Eliza, built at MIT in the mid-1960s, ran a therapy script called DOCTOR that asked users questions about their feelings and experiences—and left its creator disconcerted about his technology’s strong emotional pull. Since chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude have burst onto the scene, large swaths of the population have been using non-therapy-branded AIs for emotional and mental-health support. Two cultural forces are coming together right now: the growing embrace and destigmatization of therapy, and the idea, explicitly espoused by Silicon Valley, that AI can accomplish what patients seek. I was interested to see how these tools worked in practice, so, although I could not be a neutral observer, I signed up for Tee and attended a few sessions. After I logged in, the chatbot moved me through predetermined session stages that I could follow on my screen’s right-hand corner: Agenda Setting, Active Conversation, Core Work, Practice Plan, Session Complete. It encouraged me to talk about whatever I wanted to, but in the beginning focused on identifying a clear-cut problem, which it wanted to set as the session’s “agenda.” With the agenda set, we went back and forth a bit until the bot suggested that we “shift now from exploring the problem to building a small, realistic step forward.” Its proposed remedy was an exercise patterned on cognitive behavioral therapy that involved pausing for 90 seconds each day before I started work. These sorts of exercises can be helpful. But, in this cycle of identifying problems and fixes, we did not touch what is underneath. The chatbot was also willing to “just talk it through,” rather than offering a concrete suggestion. When we took this route, I could tell that the bot was attempting active listening—restating and asking questions about my experience, mimicking empathy. That’s a process that can help clarify thoughts, but knowing that no one was behind the dialogue, that the empathy was a technique and not a presence, left me with a sense of being poignantly unheard. Much of what matters in therapy happens in nonverbal communication. During a recent session, a patient of mine spoke flatly about upcoming social plans. Then he stopped momentarily, and his eyes softened and drifted downward. The silence that opened felt profound. After a time, I said, “I wonder what happened just there.” He took a breath and began moving into emotional territory that he had long kept out of view. Tee, meanwhile, had a different approach to silence. First, I told the chatbot about my week and how I’d been doing. It validated my emotions (“that makes sense”), asked for more detail, and around we went. But whenever I stopped typing, and might have dipped into the more meaningful recesses of myself, the chatbot in front of me was inert and lifeless. The nonverbal interplay between selves that is so important in human therapy was palpably absent. Being silent with the chatbot did not feel like an invitation to being together, but rather like a kind of deadness. I felt the strong impulse to type quickly to spur the machine back to life. There was no indication that the bot remained with me as I quietly began to feel. It is true that AI can simulate presence and empathy—sometimes fairly convincingly. That’s why people adopt chatbots as confidants and therapists in the first place. And it’s likely that future versions of the therapy bots will get better at making silence feel more meaningful. But there is a wide gulf between AI conveying I understand you and I am here with you , and AI actually being with you. Mimicking presence feels more like emotional deception. When patients trust their therapist and the therapy process, they move into a vulnerable place—and being deceived this way leads to ineffective therapy at best, and may cause harm. Most critiques of AI therapy focus on AI’s sycophancy—its failure to intervene and challenge destructive patterns of thought and action, contributing to suicides, manic episodes, and psychotic states. These critiques, while important, carry forward the old model of the therapist as a dispassionate technician. They see AI therapy as harmful because it does not act upon the patient correctly. This is a framework that the technology companies can get behind. They respond that, sure, the current chatbots have problems, but these are fixable. OpenAI and other companies have taken to publishing statistics demonstrating that their chatbots are making gains in terms of intervening with distressed users in appropriate ways. The underlying argument is that mental-health support is a set of techniques and interventions, and that once machines learn to marshal these effectively, all will be well. In my work with patients, I keep theories and techniques in mind, but the most important element of the process is striving to be fully present. If there is a North Star in this work, it is being with patients in their emotional experience in a deep and lasting way. This approach is borne out in the rich psychoanalytic literature on empathy and emotional dwelling . Trauma is most enduring when patients have felt alone in it, and one of the best pathways toward healing is coming to feel that another person remains with you in your suffering, and thus that you are no longer alone. And studies on what helps patients in therapy, across different therapeutic modalities, illustrate the importance of the human relationship and of the patient and therapist being able to express emotion . AI is an alluring alternative to traditional therapy. The barriers to entry are almost nonexistent: Gone are the friction and labor of finding a human therapist, building trust, and opening up. And AI’s promise of affordable therapy is genuinely appealing. The economics of human therapy are broken. The U.S. in particular is in profound need of insurance reform and legislation that will make therapy affordable for all. In this field as in all fields, AI is not going back into the bottle, and I imagine that it may take on useful adjunct roles in mental-health care. But AI therapy cannot meet our needs. Whatever inroads people take into AI therapy, the strongest pull, if not on the surface then as a current beneath, will be the yearning for someone who can feel with you as you move further into yourself. At the heart of AI therapy is a paradox: We embrace it out of our longing for exactly what it cannot ultimately give.

items.title: Drug trafficking: Court sentences South African woman to 25 yrs in prison
items.description: The Federal High Court in Abuja on Thursday sentenced a 38-year-old South African woman, Will Ann, to 25 years’ imprisonment for smuggling 5.75kg of heroin into Nigeria. Justice Obiora Egwuatu, in a judgment, held that Nigerian law does not respect emotions. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that Ann was arrested when she trafficked the substance through the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport in Abuja. The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) had, in August, arraigned Ann before the court where she pleaded guilty to unlawfully importing 5.75 kilogrammes of heroin into the country on July 6. The NDLEA revealed that the woman was arrested in July while travelling with her three-year-old son. She was arrested during an inward clearance of passengers on Qatar Airways Flight QR1433, arriving from Doha. Delivering the judgment, Justice Egwuatu held that prior to her guilty plea, the defendant had admitted to committing the offence in her extrajudicial statement. The judge said that the law is settled that a conviction follows a plea of guilty. Justice Egwuatu consequently convicted her of the offence. Following her conviction, the prosecution urged the court to factor in the cost of 1kg of heroin, which is worth about N18 million, in sentencing her. Ann, however, begged the court to temper justice with mercy. She promised never to engage in such an act again. She also said she was remorseful and did not know there were illicit drugs in the bag. After hearing from the parties and considering the defendant’s plea for leniency, the judge said “crime does not pay” and that the law is not influenced by “emotions.” The judge consequently sentenced her to 15 years’ imprisonment in Count 1 and 25 years’ imprisonment in Count 2. He ordered that the sentences shall run concurrently. The judge also ruled that if the convict does not appeal within the prescribed period allowed by law, the heroin should be destroyed. (NAN) The post Drug trafficking: Court sentences South African woman to 25 yrs in prison appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 134 former MMDCEs demand payment of outstanding terminal benefits from Finance Ministry
items.description: A group of former Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs) who served during the first term of former President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo has petitioned the Ministry of Finance over outstanding terminal benefits they say are owed to them. The former MMDCEs, whose service was extended until the appointment of new chief executives in October 2021, say 134 of them were not renominated for a second term but have still not received their terminal benefits. In a letter dated September 2, 2026, addressed to Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson, the group said they had pursued payment of the benefits after leaving office but were yet to receive them. The petition was signed by Leo-Nelson Adzidogah, a former Municipal Chief Executive for Akatsi South, on behalf of the affected former MMDCEs. According to the group, at the beginning of the second term of the Akufo-Addo administration, first-term MMDCEs were instructed to remain in office pending the nomination and appointment of new chief executives. They said when the new nominations were made in October 2021, 134 of the serving MMDCEs were not renominated and subsequently left office. The former MMDCEs said they initially expected their terminal benefits to be paid after the end of the second term alongside those of their successors. However, they said their successors have since received their terminal benefits while the former MMDCEs who were not renominated remain unpaid. A major concern raised in the petition relates to the period between January and October 2021. The former MMDCEs said colleagues who were renominated for a second term received benefits covering the same period during which both groups served. They argue that excluding those who were not renominated amounts to unequal treatment, particularly because the affected MMDCEs continued performing their duties until their replacements were appointed. “It is therefore unfair to leave us out while our colleagues who worked with us during the said period were paid.” The group said their departure from office before the end of the second term should not be used as a basis to deny them benefits to which they believe they are entitled. They described the situation as an oversight and appealed to the Finance Minister to review the matter and authorise payment. “We humbly believe that our exit from office during and before the end of the second term should not be used to deny us of our benefits.” The petitioners have therefore asked the Ministry of Finance to take the matter into consideration and facilitate payment of the outstanding terminal benefits. Copies of the petition were also sent to the Deputy Minister and Chief Director of the Ministry of Finance.

En términos absolutos, la vivienda se encareció 260 euros por metro cuadrado respecto al mismo periodo de 2025. items.title: Coopération Togo-Corée du Sud : La République de Corée renforce les capacités numériques des communes togolaises
items.description: Lomé, 16 sept. (ATOP) – La République de Corée a remis, le mercredi 16 septembre à Lomé, un lot d’équipements informatiques et deux groupes électrogènes au Togo, dans le cadre du renforcement de la coopération bilatérale entre les deux pays. La cérémonie officielle de remise a été marquée par la signature d’un accord de partenariat et l’échange de parapheurs entre les parties. Remise symbolique du matériel informatique D’une valeur de 299.324,32 dollars US, soit environ 162.899.412 francs CFA, le don est composé de 100 ordinateurs portables, 100 ordinateurs de bureau, 60 imprimantes et 10 scanners. Ces équipements sont destinés aux communes de Golfe 1, Kozah 1, Binah 1, Binah 2 et Kloto 3, afin de contribuer au renforcement de leurs capacités matérielles et opérationnelles. Le don comprend également deux groupes électrogènes de 80 KVA et de 100 KVA, destinés au ministère des Affaires étrangères, de la Coopération et des Togolais de l’extérieur, pour renforcer ses capacités logistiques et assurer une meilleure continuité de ses activités. Le ministre délégué auprès du ministre des Affaires étrangères, chargé de la Coopération et des Togolais de l’extérieur, Yackoley Kokou Johnson, a salué la coopération entre le Togo et la République de Corée. Il a relevé que ce don traduit la volonté de la partie coréenne d’accompagner les efforts du Togo dans le processus de modernisation de son administration et de développement des collectivités territoriales. Pour le ministre, cet appui matériel constitue également une illustration concrète des relations d’amitié et de coopération qui unissent les deux pays. Il a exprimé la reconnaissance du gouvernement togolais à la République de Corée pour son accompagnement et souhaité que cette coopération se poursuive et se diversifie au bénéfice des populations. Les groupes électrogènes L’ambassadeur de la République de Corée au Togo et au Ghana, Park Kyongsig représentant le pays donateur, a souligné l’importance de ce geste dans le cadre des relations bilatérales. Il a indiqué que la Corée entend poursuivre son accompagnement du Togo à travers des initiatives contribuant au renforcement des capacités institutionnelles et au développement socio-économique. Selon lui, les équipements remis devraient permettre aux communes bénéficiaires d’améliorer leurs moyens de travail et de renforcer la qualité des services offerts aux populations. Il a réaffirmé l’engagement de la République de Corée à maintenir des relations étroites avec le Togo et à approfondir la coopération entre les deux pays. La cérémonie s’inscrit dans le cadre des relations d’amitié et de coopération entre la République togolaise et la République de Corée, établies depuis le 26 juillet 1963 et renforcées par la signature, en 1967, d’un accord de coopération technique. À travers ce don, la coopération coréenne entend contribuer au renforcement des moyens techniques des collectivités territoriales et de l’administration togolaise. ATOP/IS/SED
